title: The Dark Side of Print
summary: Printing spread wonderful ideas, but it could also spread lies, and some rulers answered books with bonfires. Printers breathed poison from their lead letters, forests became paper, and some old library books are slowly crumbling to dust. This chapter looks at the problems printing caused and how people have fought to fix them.

sections.heading: Bonfires and Banned Books
paragraphs: So far, most of our story has been about printing as a hero: spreading Bibles, science, news and stories to millions of people. But a fair history has to look at the shadows too. The very thing that made the press so powerful, its ability to put the same words in front of thousands of readers, was exactly what made people in charge nervous. A handwritten pamphlet might reach a few friends. A printed one could reach a whole country before anyone could stop it.

Almost as soon as printing spread, rulers and church leaders tried to control it. You met the Catholic Church's Index of Prohibited Books in Chapter 13. Protestant rulers, kings and city councils made their own rules too. In many countries, printers needed a licence from the government, and books had to be checked by an official censor before they could be sold. Printing a forbidden book could mean losing your press, paying a huge fine, going to prison or worse.

Some printers paid with their lives. Étienne Dolet was a French scholar and printer in Lyon who published works that the authorities considered heretical. He was arrested several times and in 1546 he was executed in Paris, and his books were burned with him. In 1889 a statue of him was put up in Paris on the spot where he died, honoring him as a martyr for free thought, although it was melted down during the Second World War. In England, the translator William Tyndale, whose English New Testament had to be printed abroad and smuggled in, was executed in 1536.

In colonial New York, a German-born printer named John Peter Zenger was thrown in jail in 1734 because his newspaper criticized the colony's governor. At his trial in 1735, his lawyer argued that printing something true should not be a crime, and the jury agreed and set him free. The case became a famous step on the road to freedom of the press in America.

Burning books is one of the oldest ways of trying to destroy ideas. One of the most notorious book burnings in history happened in Germany on 10 May 1933, a few months after the Nazi Party came to power. It was organized mainly by the German Student Association, as the high point of a campaign it called 'Against the Un-German Spirit'. Students raided libraries and bookshops for books by Jewish writers, political opponents and anyone the Nazis disliked. Bonfires were lit in more than 20 university towns that night. In Berlin, on a square called the Opernplatz (today Bebelplatz), about 20,000 books were burned in front of a crowd of about 40,000 people, and Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels gave a speech that was broadcast on the radio. The books thrown into the flames included works by the psychologist Sigmund Freud, the novelists Thomas Mann, Stefan Zweig and Erich Maria Remarque, the poet Bertolt Brecht, and even the American writers Helen Keller, Jack London and Ernest Hemingway.

More than a century earlier, the German poet Heinrich Heine, who was himself Jewish-born, had written a line in his 1821 play 'Almansor' that is often quoted about that night: 'Where they burn books, they will in the end also burn people.' Sadly, his warning came true in the Holocaust. Today, in the middle of Bebelplatz in Berlin, there is a memorial by the artist Micha Ullman: a glass window in the ground through which you look down into an underground room of empty white bookshelves, with space for about the number of books that were burned. Heine's words are on a plaque nearby.

Censorship did not end in 1945. In many countries today, writers and journalists are still jailed for what they print, and books are still banned from libraries and schools. That is why so many people argue that the freedom to print and to read is worth protecting carefully.

sections.heading: Printed Lies and the Moon Hoax
paragraphs: A printing press does not know whether the words in it are true. It will print a lie just as neatly as a fact, and often a lie spreads faster, because it is more exciting. From the very beginning of print, people used it for propaganda: one-sided messages designed to change what people think, often by stirring up fear or anger.

During the Reformation, both sides printed woodcut cartoons showing their enemies as monsters or devils. During wars, governments printed posters to make soldiers and citizens hate the other side. Some printed material was far worse than unfair. In the 1400s and 1500s, printed pamphlets spread false stories accusing Jewish communities of terrible crimes, and these lies fed violence against real people. In the early 1900s, a forged document called 'The Protocols of the Elders of Zion' was printed in Russia, claiming to reveal a secret Jewish plan to rule the world. In 1921 the London newspaper The Times showed that large parts of it had been copied from an older French satire that had nothing to do with Jewish people at all. Even after it was proved to be a fake, it was printed again and again in many languages, and the Nazis used it in their propaganda. It is one of the clearest examples of how a printed lie can do terrible harm long after it has been exposed.

Not every printed lie is so dark. Some were hoaxes, made to fool readers and sell papers. The most famous is the Great Moon Hoax. In the summer of 1835, New York's 'The Sun', one of the new cheap 'penny papers' that sold for a single cent, began a series of six articles starting on 25 August. They claimed to be reprinted from a respected Scottish science journal and reported that the real British astronomer Sir John Herschel, working in South Africa, had used an enormous new telescope to see life on the Moon.

The details were wonderfully vivid. The telescope's lens was said to be 24 feet (over 7 meters) across and to weigh 7 tons. Through it, the articles said, Herschel had seen forests, seas and beaches, herds of bison-like animals, goats with a single horn, small zebra-like creatures, beavers that walked on two legs and built huts, and finally furry winged people, the 'man-bats', who built temples. The series ended by claiming that the observations had stopped when sunlight was focused through the giant lens and set the observatory on fire.

None of it was true. Herschel was really in South Africa studying the southern sky, but he knew nothing about the articles. The author was almost certainly a Sun reporter named Richard Adams Locke, who admitted it in 1840. Many readers believed the story, at least for a while, and newspapers across the United States and Europe reprinted it. The Sun admitted in September 1835 that the articles were made up, but never printed a proper apology. Herschel was amused at first, and later rather annoyed at having to answer questions about his supposed man-bats.

Historians still argue about exactly how many people were fooled and how much the paper's sales rose; some popular retellings probably exaggerate both. But the hoax shows something important. In 1835, ordinary people were hungry for science news, and most could not check the facts for themselves. A cheap, fast newspaper with an exciting story could reach thousands of readers in a day. The same is true today, only much faster, which is why journalists, scientists and readers all have to ask: who wrote this, and how do they know?

sections.heading: Poison in the Letters
paragraphs: Printers were often clever, well-read people, but their workshops could be dangerous places to spend a life. The biggest hidden danger was the type itself. Remember that type metal is mostly lead, mixed with tin and antimony. Lead is a poison. It does not make you sick all at once. Instead, it builds up in the body over months and years, causing stomach cramps (an old name was 'lead colic'), tiredness, headaches, weak muscles and, in serious cases, damage to the nerves and brain. Children are especially sensitive to it.

People noticed the danger early. The Italian doctor Bernardino Ramazzini, who wrote one of the first books about diseases caused by work, published around 1700, discussed the health problems of many trades. In 1786 Benjamin Franklin, who had started out as a printer, wrote a letter to his friend Benjamin Vaughan about lead. He remembered from his youth as a compositor in London in the 1720s that some printers who heated their type, for example by warming the cases near a fire, ended up with weak or painful hands, and he wrote about how long it can take for people to accept that a common substance is harmful.

Compositors picked up thousands of pieces of lead type every day with their bare fingers, and lead dust from the cases got onto their hands, their food and their clothes. Many ate and drank at their workbenches, which made it worse. Workers in type foundries, where type was cast, breathed fumes from pots of molten metal. After the Linotype arrived in the 1880s, every machine had its own little pot of hot metal bubbling beside the operator, and newspapers also melted down huge amounts of lead to cast curved printing plates for their rotary presses, a process called stereotyping.

In 1917 the American doctor Alice Hamilton, a pioneer of workplace health, and her colleague Charles Verrill published a major study called 'Hygiene of the Printing Trades' for the US government. They found lead poisoning among typesetters, metal melters and stereotypers, and called it one of the most serious problems in the industry. Their recommendations sound simple now: good ventilation, hoods over the metal pots, washrooms, separate places to eat and never eating with dirty hands. Slowly, safety rules and better habits made print shops healthier, and when hot metal type disappeared in the 1970s and 1980s, so did most of the lead.

Lead was not the only danger. Inks once contained poisonous pigments, including lead-based whites and yellows. Printers used powerful solvents to clean ink off rollers and plates, and breathing their vapors day after day could harm the liver, kidneys and nerves. As recently as the early 2010s, doctors in Japan discovered that an unusual number of young workers in the proof-printing department of a small printing company in Osaka had developed a rare cancer of the bile ducts. Investigators linked it to a cleaning solvent called 1,2-dichloropropane that the workers had breathed in heavy doses for years in a poorly ventilated room. The discovery led to new safety rules in Japan, and it reminded the world that the printing industry still has to watch the chemicals it uses very carefully.

sections.heading: Forests, Water and Paper
paragraphs: In Chapter 15 you saw how Friedrich Gottlob Keller's method of grinding wood into pulp made paper cheap enough for everyone. That was a triumph for readers, but it also meant that the world's appetite for paper would be fed by trees, in enormous numbers. Newspapers, magazines, books, catalogues, office paper, cardboard boxes and packaging all come from the same basic recipe of plant fibers and water.

Making paper from wood uses a lot of resources. Logs have to be cut, transported and either ground up or cooked with chemicals to separate the cellulose fibers from the lignin, the natural glue that holds wood together. Paper mills use huge amounts of water to carry the fibers, and a great deal of energy to run machines and dry the paper on rows of hot cylinders. The pulp and paper industry is one of the biggest industrial users of energy in many countries.

Then there is whiteness. Wood pulp is naturally brownish, the color of a paper grocery bag. To make bright white paper, mills bleach it. For much of the 1900s, many mills used chlorine gas for bleaching, and the waste water flowing into rivers contained harmful chemicals, including dioxins, which can build up in fish and animals. Scientists and campaigners raised the alarm in the 1980s, and since the 1990s most mills have switched to gentler methods such as chlorine dioxide or oxygen-based bleaches, and treat their waste water before releasing it. The rivers near many old mill towns are much cleaner now than they were fifty years ago.

Forests are the other big question. Cutting down old natural forests for pulp can destroy the homes of animals and plants. Today a large share of the wood used for paper comes from trees grown on purpose in managed plantations, or from leftover wood chips and sawdust from sawmills, and certification schemes such as the Forest Stewardship Council, founded in 1993, put labels on paper that comes from responsibly managed forests. Problems remain, but readers can help by choosing certified and recycled paper.

The best answer of all is to use paper again. Paper is one of the most recycled materials in the world. In recycling, old paper is soaked and churned in water until it falls apart back into pulp. Ink is removed by a process called deinking, often by blowing air bubbles through the pulp so that ink particles stick to the bubbles and float to the top as a gray foam that can be skimmed away. Then the clean fibers are made into new paper. Each time, the fibers get a little shorter and weaker, so they can usually be recycled only a handful of times (often quoted as about five to seven), after which they are too short to hold a sheet together. That is why some fresh fiber is usually mixed in.

The numbers are encouraging. In the United States in 2018, about 67 million tons of paper and cardboard were thrown away, and about 68 percent of it was recycled, the highest rate of any material in household trash. Corrugated cardboard boxes were recycled at a rate of over 96 percent. In Europe, the paper recycling rate reached about 79 percent in 2023. Recycling paper saves energy, water and trees, and it keeps paper out of landfills, where it can rot and release methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.

sections.heading: The Slow Fire in the Library
paragraphs: Here is a mystery that librarians discovered in the 1900s. In a great library, a book printed on rag paper in the 1500s might still have bright white, flexible pages. But a book printed in 1900, four hundred years younger, might have pages so yellow and brittle that a corner snaps off like a cracker when you turn it. What was going on?

The answer was acid. From about the middle of the 1800s until the 1980s, most paper was acidic. There were two main reasons. First, cheap paper made from ground wood still contained lignin and other substances that break down into acids, especially when exposed to light and heat. (This is why old newspapers left in the sun turn yellow so quickly.) Second, papermakers 'sized' paper, treating it so ink would not spread like on a paper towel, with a mixture of rosin and a chemical called alum. Alum is acidic, and over the years it helps create acid inside the paper.

Acid attacks the long cellulose molecules that give paper its strength, chopping them into shorter and shorter pieces. It works slowly and silently, which is why librarians call it the 'slow fire'. You cannot see flames, but year by year the paper loses its strength until it crumbles. Depending on how acidic the paper is and how warm and damp the shelves are, books can become too fragile to use in as little as 50 to 70 years. By the 1980s, a large share of the books at the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., one of the biggest libraries in the world, were thought to be too brittle for normal use.

In the 1930s and later in the 1950s, an American document restorer named William Barrow carried out careful studies showing just how badly acidic book papers were decaying. His work helped convince papermakers to change. In the 1950s chemists developed new 'alkaline' sizing that did not need alum, and by the 1980s and 1990s acid-free paper had become normal for books. Good acid-free paper is expected to last for many centuries: around 500 years for average grades and perhaps more than 1,000 years for the best. Standards were written to define 'permanent paper', including an American standard in 1984 and the international standard ISO 9706 in 1994. Books printed on such paper may carry a tiny infinity symbol inside a circle, often on the copyright page. See if you can find one in a book near you.

But what about the millions of acidic books already on library shelves? Libraries fight back in several ways. They keep books in cool, dry, dark storerooms, because heat and damp speed up the decay. They copy the most fragile books onto microfilm or scan them into digital files so that the words survive even if the paper does not. And they use mass deacidification. The Library of Congress, for example, has treated millions of books with a process in which the books are placed in large cylinders and soaked in a liquid carrying fine particles of magnesium oxide. The particles neutralize the acid and leave behind an alkaline reserve, a sort of chemical shield that keeps neutralizing new acid for years to come. Treated paper is tested to make sure it lasts several times longer than untreated paper. Deacidification cannot make brittle pages strong again, so it works best before books start to crumble.

sections.heading: When Machines Took the Jobs
paragraphs: Every big change in printing helped millions of readers, but it also hurt the workers whose skills suddenly were not needed. This has happened again and again throughout the story.

The first to feel it were the scribes. In the late 1400s, some scribes and scholars complained loudly that the new presses were churning out careless, ugly, error-filled books for anyone with money. A Venetian friar, Filippo de Strata, wrote a protest to the city's ruler in the 1470s asking for printing to be restrained. The German abbot Johannes Trithemius wrote a work called 'In Praise of Scribes' in 1492, arguing that monks should keep copying by hand because copying was good for the soul and parchment would last longer than paper. With a touch of irony, his book was then printed so that more people could read it. Copying by hand did not vanish overnight; scribes kept making fine manuscripts for wealthy customers and documents for governments for many years. But as an everyday way of making books, hand copying slowly faded away.

Four hundred years later, it was the hand compositors' turn. When the Linotype and Monotype machines arrived in the 1880s and 1890s, one operator could set type several times faster than a person picking letters from a case. Many typesetters feared for their jobs, and some did lose them. But printing was growing so fast, with bigger newspapers and more magazines, that many compositors retrained as machine operators, and printers' unions became some of the strongest trade unions in the world.

Then, in the 1960s to the 1980s, phototypesetting and computers made hot metal type itself unnecessary. Now journalists could type their stories straight into a computer, and pages could be made without anyone setting metal at all. This led to some of the bitterest labor battles in printing history. The most famous was the Wapping dispute in London. In January 1986, Rupert Murdoch's company News International moved the printing of newspapers including The Times and The Sun to a new plant at Wapping in East London, using new computer technology. About 6,000 print workers went on strike and were dismissed. The dispute, with angry picket lines outside the new plant, lasted about a year before the strike collapsed in February 1987. The new plant needed only a fraction of the old number of printers. A whole craft, with centuries of skill and tradition behind it, had almost disappeared.

Historians and economists still argue about how to weigh up these changes. New technology usually made printed things cheaper and more plentiful, and created new kinds of jobs, from machine engineers to graphic designers. But for the particular people whose skills were replaced, especially older workers, the change could be very hard. The same questions are being asked today about computers and artificial intelligence.

sections.heading: Pirates and Copycats
paragraphs: If you can print a book, you can also print someone else's book without asking. From the earliest days of print, 'pirate' printers copied successful books and sold them cheaply, without paying the author or the original publisher anything. Soon after Aldus Manutius in Venice began his popular pocket-size books in italic type, printers in Lyon in France were turning out imitations. Martin Luther complained bitterly that pirate printers rushed out sloppy, error-filled copies of his writings, sometimes even before his own printer had finished. Readers did not always know which copy was the real one.

At first, the only protection was a 'privilege', special permission from a ruler that gave one printer the right to print a certain book for a few years. Later, countries began to write copyright laws. Britain's Statute of Anne of 1710, which you met in Chapter 14, gave the right to the author for a limited time. But laws stopped at the border. For much of the 1800s, American publishers freely reprinted books by British authors without paying them. Charles Dickens, whose novels were hugely popular in the United States, toured America in 1842 and spoke out for international copyright, to the annoyance of some American newspapers. Change came slowly: the Berne Convention, an international agreement on copyright, was signed in 1886, and the United States passed a law in 1891 that began to protect foreign authors.

Copyright is a balancing act. Authors, artists and publishers need to be paid, or they cannot afford to keep creating. But readers, students and scientists also need to be able to read, quote and build on what others have written, and copyright eventually ends so that old works become free for everyone. Arguments about where the line should be have never stopped. Photocopiers raised them in the 1960s and 1970s, and the internet has made copying easier than ever before.

Looking back over this chapter, the dark side of print is mostly the dark side of people. Printing is a tool. It can spread truth or lies, free thinkers or punish them, poison workers or be made safe, destroy forests or recycle them. Many of the problems we have met were eventually tackled by doctors, scientists, librarians, campaigners and ordinary readers who refused to accept them. And just as people were learning these lessons, a new tool arrived. Then computers arrived, and printing began to leave paper behind altogether.

deepDive: Paper decay is a chemistry problem called acid hydrolysis. Cellulose is a long chain of glucose units; in the presence of acid and moisture, the bonds linking those units break, shortening the chains and reducing fiber strength. Conservators measure this with fold-endurance tests, folding a strip back and forth until it breaks, and with pH tests. The two big sources of acid in industrial-era paper were alum-rosin sizing, introduced in the early 1800s, and lignin-rich groundwood pulp, whose breakdown products are acidic and which also yellows by oxidation in light. Mass deacidification systems, such as the magnesium oxide treatment used by the Library of Congress, aim to raise pH to slightly alkaline and leave an alkaline reserve of a few percent of calcium or magnesium carbonate or oxide; accelerated-aging tests suggest treated paper can last several times longer. Critics note that treatment cannot restore lost strength and can cause slight color changes, so it is a preventive measure rather than a cure. Lead poisoning in printing is a case study in occupational medicine: the harm was described anecdotally for centuries, from Ramazzini in 1700 to Franklin in 1786, but systematic statistical study came only with investigators such as Alice Hamilton in the early 1900s, and real reform followed only once evidence was gathered. Debates about printed misinformation are also old. Historians caution against assuming that readers of the past were simply gullible; the 1835 Moon Hoax, for instance, was read by some as entertainment, and claims about its effect on the Sun's circulation are probably inflated in popular retellings. Similarly, economists studying technological unemployment in printing, from Linotype to computer typesetting, generally find that output and total employment in publishing often grew while specific crafts shrank sharply, which is why both optimistic and pessimistic accounts of automation can point to printing for evidence.
funFact: Many books printed on long-lasting acid-free paper carry a tiny infinity symbol inside a circle to show that the paper meets a permanence standard.
